1.pericope_label: Yet one plague more: the spoiling of the Egyptians

schools.summary: Render the opening verb as a pluperfect and say why it matters: now the Lord HAD said, these three verses being parenthetic and referring to a revelation made before the present interview began, which is needed to explain the confidence of Moses about the last plague. Correct the English on the second clause too, since the word rendered altogether belongs with the first: when he shall let you go altogether, he shall assuredly thrust you out hence. On the greatness of Moses, face both objections. It is a difficulty that Moses should write so of himself, since THE MAN is not a title by which writers of any time or country speak of themselves; but it is far more difficult to imagine anyone else giving him so bald and poor a designation, when to other writers he is a prophet, or a man of God, or the servant of the Lord, and never simply the man. And to the objection that VERY GREAT does not comport with his meekness, answer that it is a mere statement of fact, necessary for the proper understanding of the narrative, since Moses had come to be regarded by courtiers and Egyptians alike as a personage almost on a par with the Pharaoh they revered as a god upon earth. State the mechanism of the spoiling without apologising for it: Jehovah would make the Egyptians willing to give, and the renown Moses had acquired by his miracles would contribute to it.

Take the pluperfect and then ask how far back it reaches, rejecting the suggestion that it goes as far as the appearance in Midian, which is too remote, and referring it rather to the last time Pharaoh sent for Moses — which explains why Moses was so bold and spoke with such assurance that he would see Pharaoh's face no more. Draw the same consequence for the man himself: it was not with self-conceived confidence that he was lately so elated, but because he had been forewarned by divine revelation that the contests were near their end, and he could not have interrupted the course of his vocation unless he plainly knew he was arriving at its conclusion. Then defend the spoiling on the right ground and refuse the wrong one. Some allege that the severe labours tyrannically exacted deserved a reward, so that God justly permitted a compensation of which the people would otherwise have been defrauded; but there is no necessity for these subtleties. The sole authority of God absolves them from the charge of theft, since his decree is above all laws and his will is their rule; what God has transferred to his own people must not be counted the property of others; and if the laws of war permit victors to gather the spoil, why less allowable for God, who had overcome the Egyptians in ten illustrious battles before compelling them to surrender? As to the pretense of borrowing, the women did not lie when they asked for vessels for sacrifice, since it lay with God afterwards to devote them to other uses. And take comfort from the favour granted: men's hearts are turned either way by God, who impelled the Egyptians to hate his people and could as easily incline them to give freely what they had harshly refused.

Report the proposal that the opening verb should be read in the preterpluperfect, for the Lord HAD said, since the verses that follow appear to have been spoken at the interview of the preceding chapter; and add that if this chapter be connected with that one, and the first three verses read both in the past tense and in a parenthesis, the sense will be much more distinct and clear than it now appears. On the greatness of Moses, read it as protection rather than honour: the miracles Pharaoh and his servants had seen him work impressed them with a high opinion of his wisdom and power, and had he not appeared in their sight as a person whom it would be very dangerous to molest, we may naturally conclude that some violence would long ere this have been offered to him.

Read the spoiling as unpaid wages justly demanded. This was the last day of their servitude; their masters, who had abused them in their work, would have defrauded them of their hire and sent them away empty, while the poor Israelites were so fond of liberty that they would have been satisfied with that alone; but he that executeth righteousness and judgment for the oppressed would not let the labourers lose their wages, and ordered them to demand them at their departure. Note that God will one way or another give redress to the injured who in humble silence commit their cause to him. Then observe who did the respecting: though Pharaoh hated Moses, there were those of Pharaoh's servants that respected him — as in Caesar's household there were some who had an esteem for Paul. Those that honour God, he will honour; and however meanly they pass through this world, there is a day coming when they will look great in the eyes of all.

debates.question: How far back does the pluperfect 'the Lord had said' reach?

sides.position: To a revelation made before this interview began; the three verses are parenthetic
Not as far as the appearance in Midian, which is too remote, but to the last time Pharaoh sent for Moses
To the interview of the preceding chapter; read so, and in a parenthesis, the sense becomes much clearer

debates.question: On what ground is the spoiling of the Egyptians defensible?

sides.position: As wages: the labourers should not lose their hire, and God ordered them to demand it at their departure
On God's sole authority; the wages argument is a subtlety there is no necessity for, since what God transfers is no longer another's property

outliers.note: Alone states the wages defence in order to reject it as an unnecessary subtlety, resting the case instead on God's authority being above all laws and on the right of a victor to the spoil, and alone answers the charge of false pretences by observing that the women did not lie in asking vessels for sacrifice.

Alone argues from the bald designation 'the man' that Moses himself must have written the phrase, since no other writer ever calls him anything so poor, and alone answers the objection that 'very great' sits ill with his meekness by making it a fact necessary to the narrative.
Alone reads the greatness of Moses as his protection, concluding that violence would long since have been offered him had he not appeared a person dangerous to molest.

themes: And the Lord said unto Moses, Yet will I bring one plague more upon Pharaoh, and upon Egypt; afterwards he will let you go hence: when he shall let you go, he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether.
Speak now in the ears of the people, and let every man borrow of his neighbour, and every woman of her neighbour, jewels of silver, and jewels of gold.
And the Lord gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh’s servants, and in the sight of the people.

4.pericope_label: About midnight will I go out: the firstborn and the great cry

schools.summary: Observe first what was withheld: the particular night was not specified, so the torment of suspense was added to the pain of an unintermittent fear, though the hour itself was placed beyond doubt and was the dreadest of the twenty-four. Then give the philology and the sociology together. The Hebrew word for firstborn is applied only to males, so the announcement was that in every family the eldest son should be cut off; and in Egypt as in most countries the law of primogeniture prevailed, the eldest son being the hope and stay of the household, and the firstborn of Pharaoh bearing a title that made him hereditary crown prince. The maidservant behind the mill marks the lowest grade in the social scale as the king upon his throne marks the highest, and all alike were to suffer. On the extension of the calamity to the beasts, call it very remarkable and connect it with the Egyptian animal-worship: four animals were at all times regarded as actual incarnations of deity and objects of profound veneration, three of them bulls and one a white cow, and it is not unlikely all were required to be firstborn. And note that Pharaoh, hardened as he is, is yet allowed a place for repentance, since had he relented now the death of the firstborn and the destruction in the Red Sea might both have been escaped.

Admire the courage before expounding the threat: Moses willingly encounters the tyrant and boasts that he shall be his conqueror, and Pharaoh must have been confounded with terror, since though so cruelly repulsed he yet dismissed the Prophet in safety. On the range of the victims, note the order — the firstborn of Pharaoh, who would have been heir of the kingdom, placed in the first rank, and afterwards the whole body of humbler people, the maid-servants who turned the revolving mills occupying a very low and despised condition, as appears from the ancient poets and from Scripture itself. But forbid the question that presses hardest. Why God, in inflicting punishment on the children, postponed till another time that of the fathers, whose sin was greater; and why, in wreaking vengeance on the beasts, he spared men — it is not our province curiously to inquire, because it is sinful to prescribe to God, whose incomprehensible wisdom surmounts all human understanding, what the rule or measure of his judgments should be. By bringing children and beasts to punishment he represented clearly to the wicked despisers of his power what they had themselves deserved. And on the disease, take it for sudden and immediate death, universal through the kingdom, inflicted by a destroying angel — very probably the pestilence.

Refuse to magnify a question that does not matter. Whether God did this by the ministry of a good or of an evil angel is of little importance, though some commentators have made much of it: both kinds are under his power and jurisdiction and he may employ them as he pleases; and though such a work of destruction is supposed more proper for a bad angel than a good one, the works of God's justice are not less holy and pure than the works of his mercy, so that the highest archangel may with the utmost propriety be employed in either. Then spend the labour where it will do good, on the mill. The portable millstones are still used in many parts of the east, the upper one turned by a lever fixed in the rim; a drawing of such a machine as used in China shows the grinder pushing the lever and running round with the stone. And a traveller reports that when the stone is large a second person is called in, the women seating themselves opposite each other with the stone between them — which explains at once both the propriety of the phrase BEHIND THE MILL and the force of the saying elsewhere that two women shall be grinding at the mill, the one taken and the other left. Add that these mills were used among our own ancestors under another name, and survive still in the northern islands.

Insist on the agent the text names: Moses and Aaron were not ordered to summon this plague, for God says I WILL GO OUT — and what is hell but to fall into the hands of the living God? Read the whole sequence as evidence of how slow God is to wrath and how willing to have his anger turned away: this stroke was threatened first and executed last, less judgments having been tried which, had they done the work, would have prevented it; and if the death of their cattle had humbled and reformed them, their children would have been spared. But if men will not improve the gradual advances of divine judgments, they must thank themselves if they find that the worst was reserved for the last. On the manner of it, note that they should not die silently and insensibly, so as not to be discovered till morning, but so as to rouse the families at midnight to stand by and see them die; and on its extent, that the prince who was to succeed in the throne was not too high to be reached by it, nor the slaves at the mill too low to be taken notice of.

debates.question: Who executes the death of the firstborn?

sides.position: God himself: Moses and Aaron were not ordered to summon this plague, for he says 'I will go out'
A destroying angel, inflicting a disease, very probably the pestilence
Whether by a good or an evil angel is of little importance; the highest archangel may with propriety be employed in a work of justice

debates.question: Why were the firstborn of the beasts included?

sides.position: Probably because of the Egyptian animal-worship, four animals being regarded as actual incarnations of deity and likely required to be firstborn
It is not our province curiously to inquire; it is sinful to prescribe to God the measure of his judgments

outliers.note: Alone stops on the mill and stays there, describing the portable millstones and the lever, citing a drawing of the Chinese machine and a traveller's account of two women seated opposite each other with the stone between them, which explains both 'behind the mill' here and the saying elsewhere that two women shall be grinding at the mill.

Alone connects the death of the firstborn of beasts with the Egyptian animal-worship, naming the four creatures venerated as incarnations of deity; and alone observes that by withholding the particular night the threat added the torment of suspense to the fear.

Alone forbids the two questions the passage most invites — why the children suffered before the fathers whose sin was greater, and why beasts were struck while men were spared — on the ground that it is sinful to prescribe to God the measure of his judgments.

themes: And Moses said, Thus saith the Lord, About midnight will I go out into the midst of Egypt:

And all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of beasts.
And there shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there was none like it, nor shall be like it any more.

7.pericope_label: Not a dog shall move his tongue; and he went out in a great anger

schools.summary: Dispose of the dogs in a line: the expression is evidently proverbial. Then supply the scene the words predict, since the details are given more fully and graphically here than in the later narrative. The servants meant are the high officers of the court who were standing about Pharaoh, and these grandees would come to Moses when the blow fell, prostrate themselves before him as if he were their king, and beseech him to take his departure with all his nation. On the closing phrase, render it in the heat of anger. And on the last two verses, note that they bring to a close the account of Moses' negotiations with Pharaoh which began several chapters earlier.

Give both senses of the dogs and decline to choose between them. Taken literally, it was a very extraordinary thing that a dog, which barks at the least noise made at night, should not sharpen his tongue when six hundred thousand men besides women and children set out with their flocks and herds, and must have marched through many places where dogs were before they came to the Red sea. Taken figuratively, it means that no Egyptian, however spiteful and ill disposed toward the children of Israel, should offer to hurt them. Then mark where Moses passes from reporting God's words to speaking in his own person, and how much that costs the tyrant: the asperity wounded him, for it was the same as if Moses had said that thus far he had entreated leave for the people to depart, but now, whether Pharaoh would or not, he would freely go, and not without the request of Pharaoh himself. On the heat of anger, hold that the servants of God, even when they truly and faithfully perform their duty, are so disturbed with indignation against sin that they are by no means restrained from being affected with anger, and that Moses was thus excited by the impulse of the Spirit, which awakened the zeal and at the same time moderated it, so that it contained no admixture of unregulated passion. Yet since we are naturally too prone to impetuous passions, the spirit of gentleness and propriety must be asked of God to prevent all excess. And let the anger of Moses prove that God would not have us lazily and coldly perform the duties he entrusts to us, so that nothing is more preposterous than for certain cynics, who jokingly philosophize about the doctrines of religion and sting God's servants with laughing and wanton witticisms, to deride a vehemence rather worthy of the highest praise.

Report the received reading of the dogs and then go beyond it. The clause has generally been understood as proverbial, meaning that the Israelites should depart without any kind of molestation, since though there must be much bustle in the sudden removal of six hundred thousand persons with their wives and goods and cattle, it should produce so little alarm that not even the dogs would bark. But hazard a conjecture. Is the allusion not to the known custom of dogs howling where there is a mortality — which is to be attributed not to any prescience but to the exquisite keenness of their scent? Dogs were sacred in Egypt and so religiously preserved in great multitudes, and the son of one of the chief deities was worshipped under the form of a dog, or a man with a dog's head, the barking Anubis, who had a temple in a city the Greeks called the city of the dog, where the sacred animals were fed with consecrated victuals. So the great cry through all the land may be that very howling, while among the Israelites there was no death and therefore no dog moved his tongue: the object of Egyptian worship deploring a calamity it had no power to prevent, and powerless to punish the worshippers of Jehovah. Thus as the magicians were confounded in the first plagues, in this last their gods were put to flight. Then attack the English of the ninth verse. Shall and will are both reputed signs of the future and used indiscriminately by many, but they make an essential difference here: SHALL NOT HEARKEN strongly intimates that it was impossible for Pharaoh to hearken and that God had placed him under that impossibility, whereas WILL NOT HEARKEN agrees with the many earlier passages where he is said to have hardened his own heart, proving that he obstinately refused without any impulsive necessity, and that God took advantage of that obstinacy to work another miracle and multiply his wonders. And report the state of the text, since the Samaritan copies here are fuller and better connected: the eighth verse has no natural connection with the seventh in the received Hebrew, contrary to the custom of Moses, who always notes where his discourses begin; the Samaritans could have had no private interest in adding what they have; and across five chapters the Hebrew gives each of seven judgment-speeches once where the Samaritan gives it twice, God commanding and Moses then delivering.

Read the silence of the dogs as an earnest of the last day: while angels drew their swords against the Egyptians, there should not so much as a dog bark at any of the children of Israel, and did men know what a difference God puts, and will put to eternity, between those that serve him and those that serve him not, religion would not seem to them such an indifferent thing as they make it. On the submission of Pharaoh's servants, note that the proud enemies of God and his Israel shall be made to fall under at last. Then account for the anger of the meekest of all the men of the earth: probably Moses expected that the very threatening of the death of the firstborn would induce compliance, especially as Pharaoh had complied so far already and had seen how exactly all the predictions hitherto were fulfilled; but his proud heart would not yield, no, not to save all the firstborn of his kingdom. Moses was hereupon provoked to a holy indignation, being grieved, as our Saviour afterwards was, for the hardness of his heart; and it is a great vexation to the spirits of good ministers to see people deaf to all the fair warnings given them. To be angry at nothing but sin is the way not to sin in anger. Finally, take the outcome as proof: Moses did all these wonders before Pharaoh, who was himself an eye-witness of them, and yet could not prevail, which was a certain sign that God himself had, in a way of righteous judgment, hardened his heart.

debates.question: Is 'not a dog shall move his tongue' proverbial or literal?

sides.position: It may be either: literally a marvel when six hundred thousand marched out, or figuratively that no Egyptian should offer them hurt
Proverbial by common account, but perhaps an allusion to dogs howling at a mortality — and so a stroke against the dog-god of Egypt

debates.question: Does 'Pharaoh shall not hearken' mean he could not, or that he would not?

sides.position: Would not: 'shall' wrongly implies an impossibility God imposed, where the earlier chapters say Pharaoh hardened his own heart and God took advantage of the obstinacy
That Moses did all these wonders and could not prevail was a certain sign that God himself had, in righteous judgment, hardened his heart

outliers.note: Alone turns the silence of the dogs into a polemic against Egyptian religion, conjecturing an allusion to dogs howling at a mortality and identifying the barking dog-god whose worshippers he could neither help nor avenge; and alone sets out the case for the Samaritan text of this chapter, which gives each judgment-speech twice where the Hebrew gives it once.

Alone defends the anger of Moses as awakened and at the same time moderated by the Spirit, while warning that we are too prone to impetuous passions; and alone rounds on the cynics who philosophize jokingly about religion and deride a vehemence worthy of the highest praise.

Alone notes that the scene of the courtiers' submission is given more fully and graphically in this prediction than in the narrative that afterwards records it, with the grandees prostrating themselves before Moses as if he were their king.

themes: But against any of the children of Israel shall not a dog move his tongue, against man or beast: that ye may know how that the Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.

And all these thy servants shall come down unto me, and bow down themselves unto me, saying, Get thee out, and all the people that follow thee: and after that I will go out. And he went out from Pharaoh in a great anger.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Pharaoh shall not hearken unto you; that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.
And Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh: and the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, so that he would not let the children of Israel go out of his land.
